name: Asvatha
title: Son of Haman, the Agagite
summary: In the Persian Empire under King Ahasuerus, Haman's ten sons stood at the center of the dramatic conflict between Agagite Haman and the Jewish people. Asjvat was one of these sons. When Haman's conspiracy to commit genocide against the Jews was exposed through Queen Esther's courageous intervention, and Haman himself was executed, it was still not the end of the threat. The Jews received royal permission to defend themselves against their enemies, and in the battle within Susa's citadel, Haman's ten sons, including Asjvat, were killed. Their bodies were then publicly hanged at Esther's request. The account of Asjvat's fall is part of the Purim story and illustrates how God's providence turned a seemingly hopeless situation into victory for His people in the Persian diaspora.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Plan to Destroy the Jews
keyEvents.description: Haman, son of Hammedatha, planned to destroy all the Jews in the Persian Empire after a conflict with Mordecai. The king issued an edict allowing the massacre of the Jews.

keyEvents.title: Esther's Intercession for Her People
keyEvents.description: Queen Esther risked her life by going to King Ahasuerus to expose Haman's evil plan and save the Jewish people.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Execution
keyEvents.description: Haman, son of Hammedatha, was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai after his evil plan was exposed.

keyEvents.title: The Jews' Victory Over Their Enemies
keyEvents.description: The Jews were allowed to defend themselves against their enemies. In the citadel of Susa, they killed five hundred men, including Haman's ten sons.

keyEvents.title: Hammedatha and His Brothers Are Killed
keyEvents.description: Hammedatha is named among the ten sons of Haman who were killed when the Jews defended themselves in the citadel of Susa. Their death marked the complete destruction of the threat against the Jewish people.

keyEvents.title: The Sons of Haman Are Hanged
keyEvents.description: At Queen Esther's request, the bodies of Haman's ten sons, including Hammedatha, were hanged on gallows as a public testimony that the threat to the Jews was over.

versions.summary: Ashtav was one of the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, an enemy of the Jewish people in the Persian Empire. He was killed along with his brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their foes, as described in the Book of Esther. His death marked God's protection of His people during the exile.
versions.title: Son of Haman
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Son of Haman' is correct but could have been more descriptive, e.g., 'Son of Haman the Agagite,' to provide more context.; [minor] The events in the book of Esther are usually dated to around 480–470 BC under Ahasuerus (Xerxes I). '400s BC' is technically within this range, but 'c. 5th century BC' or 'c. 480s BC' would be more precise.; [major] The role 'warrior' is not supported by the text. Asjvat is mentioned only as one of Haman's ten sons who were killed. There is no indication in the book of Esther that he was a warrior. A more appropriate role would be 'son of Haman' or possibly 'official' (given his father's position), but even that is speculative.; [minor] The summary is good, but the phrasing 'in exile times' is somewhat imprecise. The events in the book of Esther take place in the Persian diaspora, not during the actual exile (which technically ended with Cyrus's decree around 538 BC). The wording should be adjusted.; [minor] There are many events that primarily concern Haman and Esther rather than Asjvat directly. For a profile on Asjvat, it could have focused more on the events where he is actually mentioned (Est 9:7–10 and 9:13–14).; [major] Footnotes are missing. Notes should be added regarding, for example, the meaning of the name Asjvat, the Jewish tradition of reading the names of Haman's sons in one breath during Purim celebrations, and the historical context.

versions.summary: Ashtav was one of the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, a great enemy of the Jewish people in the Persian Empire under King Ahasuerus. When Haman's plan to destroy the Jews was uncovered by Queen Esther, and Haman himself was executed, his ten sons were also killed as the Jews defended themselves against their enemies in the citadel of Susa. Ashtav is named among those who were slain. This event is a central part of the Purim story and testifies to God's protection of His people in the Persian diaspora.
versions.title: Son of Haman, the Agagite
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is good, but since there is an earlier version with similar wording, the text should be varied more to avoid repetition. The current version begins with nearly identical phrasing as version 1. Suggests a reworked introduction offering a somewhat different perspective.; [minor] The description mentions 'five hundred men,' but it could be clarified that this occurred in the citadel of Susa, which is already noted, though it is worth emphasizing the context more clearly.

footnotes.text: The name Ashtav (Hebrew: אַשְׁוָת, 'Ashvat') has uncertain etymology. Some scholars have suggested a Persian origin, possibly related to the Old Iranian word for 'horse' or 'strength,' but this remains debated.

In Jewish tradition, the names of Haman's ten sons (Est 9:7–10) are read in the synagogue during the Purim celebration in a single breath. This emphasizes that they were all killed at once and symbolizes the complete destruction of the enemy.

The events in the Book of Esther take place in Susa (Shushan), the Persian winter capital. Archaeological excavations at Susa have uncovered the royal palace, which matches the descriptions in the Book of Esther, including the great columned hall and the inner courtyards.

The designation 'Agagite' regarding Haman links him to Agag, king of the Amalekites (1 Sam 15). Rabbinic tradition views the conflict between Mordecai (from the tribe of Benjamin, like Saul) and Haman (the Agagite) as a continuation of the ancient enmity between Israel and Amalek.

The fact that Haman's sons were hanged (Est 9:13–14) was in line with Persian practice, where bodies were publicly displayed as a deterrent. The Hebrew word 'talah' used here can mean both hanging and impaling on a pole.

King Ahasuerus is commonly identified with Xerxes I (486–465 BC), who ruled the Achaemenid Empire at its height. The events in the Book of Esther are dated to his reign, placing Ashtav's death around 473 BC.
